column1: # Golden vectors for SRS 7.2's latch.item_key -- the DATE-FREE TITLE it is derived from.
# SRS v1.11 promised this file: "a vector file for date-free titles should be added when the
# second client is built, and until then FR-804 should be understood as reliable within a
# client and unproven across them." The second client exists, so here it is -- but the reason
# it exists has changed, and the change is worth reading before relying on it.
# WHAT THIS FILE IS NOT FOR ANY MORE. The Android and Windows clients do not have two
# implementations of this derivation. Both contain the byte-identical line
#     itemKey = itemKeyOf(itemKeyTitle(captured, result))
# and both itemKeyTitle and itemKeyOf are compiled from :wire, from this same source tree.
# Two clients running one function cannot disagree, so between those two there is no drift
# for a vector file to catch.
# WHAT IT IS FOR.
#  1. The THIRD client. SRS 4.1 names a Chrome extension, which will not be a JVM and will
#     therefore be an independent implementation -- the situation v1.11 was written about.
#     That client must reproduce every digest below or FR-804 stops working across it.
#  2. Pinning this derivation against CHANGE OVER TIME, which shared code does nothing about.
#     SRS 7.2 writes metadata once at insert and never recomputes it, so every item already in
#     a user's account carries a key derived by the code as it stood that day. A "tidier"
#     derivation would orphan all of them: FR-804 would stop matching anything written before
#     the change, and would create duplicates rather than offering to move items.
# THAT SECOND POINT HAS TEETH, AND THREE ROWS BELOW SHOW IT. two_dates and
# punctuation_after_blank keep a stray " ." where a date was blanked out, and plain_event ends
# on a dangling "at". All read badly and all are FROZEN: the key is never shown to anyone, and
# repairing them would change the identity of every item ever written.
# Columns: name <TAB> input <TAB> expected date-free title <TAB> expected sha-256 of item_key
# The third column is the point of the file. A table of inputs and digests alone would be
# unreviewable -- a wrong expectation and a right one look identical -- and this project has
# already recorded what that costs: "a test can pin behaviour exactly and pin the wrong
# behaviour". The middle column is human-legible, so every row can be read and judged.
# It was worth doing. Generating this file on 3 Sep 2026 found a real defect on its first run:
# "Renewal 2027-10-14" produced the title "Renewal 2027-" and the date 14 October 2026 -- the
# day-first pattern had matched the trailing "10-14", found no year on it and filled in the
# current one, while a correct year sat in the text. The leftover "2027-" then travelled in the
# key, so rescheduling such an item across a year boundary would have written a duplicate.
# Fixed in NumericDateRule before these vectors were taken; year_first and
# reschedule_across_years below are the rows that hold it fixed.
# The input and title columns are escaped and this file is pure ASCII by design, so that an
# editor normalising Unicode on save cannot silently turn one case into another.
# Escapes: backslash-n, backslash-t, backslash-uXXXX, backslash-backslash. Decode before use.
# Blank lines and lines beginning # are ignored.
# Clock for every row: 2026-09-03T09:00. No row depends on it -- a date's SPAN is its position
# in the text, which is the same whatever day it is read on -- and ItemKeyAcrossClientsTest
# proves that separately for the clock, the time zone, the date order and the event duration.
# The ordinary case. Note the dangling "at": cosmetic, frozen, see above.
plain_event
# A numeric date carrying a year.
numeric_date
# The same message without one. FR-503: a missing year is the current year.
numeric_no_year
# ISO 8601. The defect this file found on its first run; see the note above.
year_first
# The same shape with slashes, as an exported spreadsheet writes it.
year_first_slash
# FR-502. Both ends are blanked, not only the opening date.
range
# SRS 7.2's own example. 12 Sep 2026 is a Saturday, so the writer is wrong --
weekday_corroboration
#   and the weekday is absorbed anyway, so these two rows MUST share a digest.
weekday_absent
# FR-804's whole mechanism: these two rows MUST share a digest, or moving a
reschedule_before
#   meeting creates a second item instead of offering to move the first.
reschedule_after
# And so must this row and year_first, or a renewal cannot be rescheduled.
reschedule_across_years
# FR-506 row 3: a time with no day still has a span, and it is blanked.
time_only
# SRS 1.23: EVERY span is blanked, not only the primary. Stray " ." frozen.
two_dates
column2: PTM on 14 September 2026. Fees due 20 September 2027.

column1: # The full stop the date stood in front of. Frozen; see above.
punctuation_after_blank
# FR-206: a subject line is step 1 of the derivation and is used verbatim.
subject_wins
# NFR-404. "kal 4 baje" is a date and a time; both spans go.
hinglish_relative
# FR-503 vernacular. "3 tarikh" is the third of the month.
hinglish_tarikh
column2: 3 tarikh ko fees jama karni hai

column1: # AC-03. Nothing to blank, so the title is the whole message.
no_date_at_all
# The script Android bundles a model for and Windows may have no pack for.
devanagari
# FR-503 offsets: "within 2 weeks" is a date span like any other.
offset
